bib.title: Think Deep, Not Just Long: Measuring LLM Reasoning Effort via Deep-Thinking Tokens

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Think Deep, Not Just Long: Measuring LLM Reasoning Effort via Deep-Thinking Tokens", Wei-Lin Chen (UVA / Google), Liqian Peng, Tian Tan, Chao Zhao, Blake JianHang Chen, Ziqian Lin, Alec Go, Yu Meng. Preprint, arXiv:2602.13517v2 [cs.CL], dated 6 Jul 2026 (Google copyright; no peer-reviewed venue stated).

COVERAGE: 23 pages, 69,314 chars. I read about 67,800 chars: the main text, tables, appendices A to E, and the references (skimmed). I did not read chars ~52,000-53,500, which is the start of Appendix A (the KL and cosine metric definitions). The next paragraph states the Appendix A results, which I did read. No scanned or garbled pages. The Qwen3-4B Think@n row in Table 2 is partly interleaved in the extraction.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Token count correlates negatively with accuracy on average, while DTR correlates positively.
 number: token count mean r = -0.59 (Table 1 average -0.594); DTR r = 0.687; Figure 1 on GPT-OSS-120B-medium: -0.544 vs 0.828.
 setup: 8 model variants (GPT-OSS-20B/120B at low/medium/high, DeepSeek-R1-70B (a Llama-3.3-70B distill), Qwen3-30B-Thinking) x 4 benchmarks (AIME 24/25, HMMT 25, GPQA-D). 25 samples per question, neutral "reason step by step" prompt, no budget. Pearson r over 5 quantile bins of accuracy; averaged over 30 seeds.
 quote: "token count exhibit notable oranged-colored values (r <0), with mean r=−0.59. This indicates that longer generations are more associated with lower performance"; "achieving the highest average correlation of r = 0.687"
 where: p.8; Table 1 p.7; Fig 1 p.1

2. DTR beats confidence baselines on average but is not uniformly positive. Confidence metrics are heterogeneous.
 number: confidence means 0.219 (neg. perplexity) to 0.605 (self-certainty); DTR is negative in 2 of 32 settings. From Table 1: OSS-20B-medium on AIME24 is -0.192, Qwen3-30B on AIME24 is -0.657, and OSS-120B-low on HMMT is only 0.305.
 quote: "confidence-based measures ... exhibit moderately positive correlations with mean r= 0.219∼ 0.605"; "exhibiting the fewest orange-colored values (2 out of the 32 model–benchmark settings tested)"
 where: p.8; Table 1 p.7

3. Reverse token count has the same magnitude as token count, but the authors call it only a post hoc statistical adjustment. It is not a principled effort measure.
 number: +0.594 average
 quote: "Reversing token count yields a positive correlation of identical magnitude. However, the improvement is purely post hoc"
 where: p.8

4. Think@n matches or beats self-consistency at about half the cost.
 number: OSS-120B-medium, AIME25: Think@n 94.7% at 155.4k tokens (-49%) vs Cons@n 92.7% at 307.6k. AIME24: 93.3 vs 92.7. HMMT25: 80.0 vs 80.0. GPQA-D: 74.7 vs 73.8. Qwen3-4B-Thinking: Think@n 90.0 / 93.3 / 66.7 / 69.7 at -50% on all four, vs Cons@n 86.7 / 93.3 / 63.3 / 67.8. Self-Certainty@n at similar cost is lower on 3 of 4 (e.g. AIME25 87.3).
 setup: n=48 samples, keep top eta=50%, prefix of 50 tokens used to score DTR, results averaged over 10 trials. Cost counts total generated tokens, including the prefix overhead for discarded samples. Only 2 models were tested for Think@n.
 quote: "Think@n consistently matches or exceeds the accuracy of Cons@n while requiring approximately half the inference cost."
 where: p.10 (Table 2), p.12; Fig 5 p.11

5. Length-based selection is a weak heuristic.
 number: OSS-120B-medium AIME25: Mean@n 80.0, Long@n 86.7, Short@n 87.3 (-17% cost), vs Cons@n 92.7. Short@n saves only 7 to 18% of cost.
 quote: "Short@n achieves modest cost savings relative to Cons@n, yet consistently underperforms it in accuracy. Long@n exhibits further degraded performance compared to Short@n without offering any cost-saving benefits."
 where: p.12, Table 2

6. A 50-token prefix is enough to rank samples by DTR.
 number: AIME25, OSS-120B-medium: prefix 50 gives 94.7 at 155.4k; 100 gives 92.0; 500 gives 92.7; 1000 gives 92.7 at 177.4k; 2000 gives 92.0 at 198.8k; full sequence gives 94.0 at 307.6k. Pass@1 is 80.0 and Cons@n is 90.0 in Table 3 (Table 2 says 92.7 for the same cell, which is inconsistent).
 quote: "using only ℓprefix = 50 tokens achieves higher accuracy than longer prefixes and matches the performance obtained using the full sequence" (the authors call this a "preliminary ablation" on AIME 25 only)
 where: p.11, Table 3

7. Higher reasoning-level settings give lower DTR but better accuracy. DTR is not comparable across models or modes.
 number: none (Fig 7 shows within-level correlations: AIME25 0.937 / 0.849 / 0.769 for low / medium / high; GPQA-D 0.980 / 0.871 / 0.839)
 setup: GPT-OSS-120B, same weights, only the system prompt differs
 quote: "lower reasoning-level configurations exhibit higher DTR values, whereas higher reasoning-level configurations yield systematically smaller DTR while achieving better task accuracy." Also: "This also suggests DTR might not be directly comparable across different models or model modes."
 The authors' hypothesis (not tested) is that higher levels "redistribute computation from depth to sequence length".
 where: p.18-19, Fig 7 p.20

8. The distance metric matters. JSD is best.
 number: AIME25 / HMMT25 correlations: JSD 0.869 / 0.895; cosine 0.633 / 0.172; KL -0.698 / 0.409. Setup: OSS-120B-medium.
 quote: "JSD-based DTR consistently achieves the strongest positive correlation with accuracy (r = 0.869 on AIME 25; r = 0.895 on HMMT 25)"
 where: p.18

9. The result depends on the settling threshold g and is less sensitive to depth fraction rho.
 number: g=0.25 gives r=0.012 (flat); g=0.5 gives 0.962; g=0.75 gives 0.820. rho in {0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95} gives r = 0.916 / 0.962 / 0.947 / 0.979. Defaults g=0.5, rho=0.85. The panel-to-r mapping is from the plot labels.
 setup: GPQA-D, GPT-OSS-20B-high only (one cell)
 quote: "a softer threshold of g= 0.25 yields a flatter trend with lower correlation value"
 where: p.9, Fig 4

10. Think@n tuning: gains grow with n and peak at eta=50%.
 number: n in {16, 32, 48}; eta in {25, 50, 75}%. Exact accuracies are not printed, only plotted.
 quote: "Performance peaks at η=50%, while decrease for a smaller fraction (η=25%) and a larger fraction (η=75%)."
 where: p.19-20

11. Qualitative case: an incorrect answer was longer and had lower DTR.
 number: incorrect 27,724 tokens, DTR 13.9%; correct 3,725 tokens, DTR 19.0%. One AIME25 problem, OSS-120B-medium. The long trace ends with a guess ("Given limited time, I will output placeholder ... 207").
 quote: "the incorrect output is substantially more verbose (27,724 tokens) and exhibits a lower DTR value (13.9), whereas the correct output is much more concise (3,725 tokens) and achieves a higher DTR value (19.0)."
 where: p.21-23

12. Mechanism, from the Fig 2 caption: templated tokens settle early; operator completions and answer tokens settle late.
 number: none
 quote: "Functional and templated words ... often converge at relatively shallow layers; Completions after operators (e.g., “+”, “=”) and answer tokens/symbols (e.g., “13”, “(D)”) do not settle until deeper layers."
 where: p.3

13. Motivation from earlier work: length is an unreliable proxy.
 number: none
 quote: "increased generation length does not consistently correlate with accuracy and may instead signal 'overthinking'". Cited: inverted-U (Wu et al. 2025), inverse scaling (Gema et al. 2025).
 where: abstract p.1, p.2

LIMITS
- It is correlational, using binned quantiles of sampled sequences. It does not show that raising DTR causes better answers. No intervention steers a model to increase DTR. The conclusion only suggests "inducing deeper ... reasoning" as future work.
- It needs white-box access to per-layer hidden states and the unembedding matrix, so it cannot be applied to API-only models. Only open-weight models were tested (GPT-OSS, DeepSeek-R1-70B distill, Qwen3-30B and Qwen3-4B).
- The benchmarks are math and graduate-level science (AIME, HMMT, GPQA-D). Nothing covers code, agents, open-ended tasks or long-context tasks.
- Think@n was tested on only 2 models. The prefix ablation used AIME25 only. The g and rho sweep used one model and one benchmark.
- The Table 1 pattern is inconsistent: DTR is negative in 2 of 32 settings and weak in others (0.161, 0.305). Averages hide this.
- Correlations come from 5 bins of data. The 5-bin protocol also gives a mean accuracy per bin, so r can be high with little data.
- The authors concede DTR is not comparable across models or reasoning modes. Within one model, DTR drops as the reasoning level rises, while accuracy rises.
- Hyperparameters g=0.5 and rho=0.85 were fixed for all runs. The authors found the result sensitive to g.
- The authors also note that early-settling tokens are not necessarily suboptimal.
- It does not address prompting. The prompt is a fixed neutral "reason step by step" instruction, and the paper never tests prompts that ask for more or less thinking.

BUILDS ON
- Logit lens, Nostalgebraist (2020): project intermediate hidden states through the unembedding matrix.
- Tuned lens, Belrose et al. (2023).
- DoLa, Chuang et al. (2023): JSD between layers.
- Early exit: Elbayad et al. (2019), Schuster et al. (2022), Teerapittayanon et al. (2016).
- Inverse scaling in test-time compute, Gema et al. (2025): protocol of multiple samples and binned correlation.
- Overthinking: Wu et al. (2025), Feng et al. (2025).
- Self-consistency, Wang et al. (2023).
- Shortest-chain voting, Hassid et al. (2025); first-finish search, Agarwal et al. (2025).
- Self-Certainty, Kang et al. (2025).
- Deep Think with Confidence, Fu et al. (2025): best-of-n protocol.
- Csordás et al. (2025) and Gupta et al. (2025) on how models use depth.

CODE: Algorithm 1 (p.4) is pseudocode. Key lines:
 D_{t,l} = JSD(p_{t,L}, p_{t,l});
 c_t = min{l : min_{j<=l} D_{t,j} <= g};
 if c_t >= ceil(rho*L) then C += 1;
 return C/|S|
Defaults g=0.5, rho=0.85. Prompts (Table 4, p.21): "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}." Table 5 is the GPQA multiple-choice prompt.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): scatter of token count vs accuracy (avg r = -0.544) next to DTR vs accuracy (avg r = 0.828). It is the headline result.
- Fig 2 (p.3): per-token layer-by-layer JSD heatmap. It shows which tokens "think deeply".
- Fig 3 (p.4): the DTR procedure on a 10-layer example.
- Fig 5 (p.11): accuracy-vs-cost Pareto plot of the aggregation methods.
- Fig 7 (p.20): DTR by GPT-OSS reasoning level. It is useful for the note on reasoning-effort settings.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction is clean, apart from Table 2 where the Qwen3-4B row is interleaved with the section heading. The Table 3 Cons@n value (90.0) differs from the Table 2 value (92.7) for the same model and benchmark, and the paper does not explain why. Fig 4 r-value to line mapping is read from plot labels and is not explicit. Ledger relevance for note 07: the paper supports "longer reasoning is not better reasoning". The "reasoning effort" setting is not tested as a prompt lever, only via the system prompt level in the GPT-OSS DTR analysis (Appendix B).
